section.title: Achan's Sin
section.sectionRationale: After the triumph of Jericho comes a shocking defeat. One man, Achan, has secretly taken what was devoted to the LORD, and because of that hidden sin all Israel is defeated at little Ai. God exposes the sin, Achan is identified and confesses, and judgment falls. It is one movement, the tragedy of Achan, which teaches the deadly seriousness of sin, the corporate nature of the covenant community, and the holiness of the God who dwells among His people.
section.thesis: Sin is never merely private: one man's hidden theft of what belonged to God brings defeat and death on the whole community, revealing that the LORD who fights for Israel is holy, that His people are bound together, and that unconfessed sin must be exposed and dealt with before God will again be with them.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the hidden sin and the defeat at Ai, verses 1 to 5; Joshua's anguished prayer and God's answer, verses 6 to 15; the exposing of Achan, verses 16 to 21; and the judgment in the Valley of Achor, verses 22 to 26.

units.label: The hidden sin and the defeat at Ai
units.note: the anger of the LORD burned against Israel

verses.text: The Israelites, however, acted {{maal|unfaithfully}} regarding the things devoted to destruction. Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of what was set apart. So the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites.
Meanwhile, Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven to the east of Bethel, and told them, “Go up and spy out the land.” So the men went up and spied out Ai.

On returning to Joshua, they reported, “There is no need to send all the people; two or three thousand men are enough to go up and attack Ai. Since the people of Ai are so few, you need not wear out all our people there.”
So about three thousand men went up, but they fled before the men of Ai.

And the men of Ai struck down about thirty-six of them, chasing them from the gate as far as the quarries and striking them down on the slopes. So the hearts of the people melted and became like water.

units.label: Joshua's prayer and God's answer
units.note: Israel has sinned; you cannot stand until you remove it

verses.text: Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell facedown before the ark of the LORD until evening, as did the elders of Israel; and they all sprinkled dust on their heads.

“O, Lord GOD,” Joshua said, “why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be destroyed? If only we had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan!
O Lord, what can I say, now that Israel has turned its back and run from its enemies?
When the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear about this, they will surround us and wipe out our name from the earth. Then what will You do for Your great name?”
But the LORD said to Joshua, “Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face?

Israel has sinned; they have transgressed My covenant that I commanded them, and they have taken some of what was {{cherem|devoted to destruction}}. Indeed, they have stolen and lied, and they have put these things with their own possessions.

This is why the Israelites cannot stand against their enemies. They will turn their backs and run from their enemies, because they themselves have been set apart for destruction. I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction.

Get up and consecrate the people, saying, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Among you, O Israel, there are things devoted to destruction. You cannot stand against your enemies until you remove them.

In the morning you must present yourselves tribe by tribe. The tribe that the LORD selects shall come forward clan by clan, and the clan that the LORD selects shall come forward family by family, and the family that the LORD selects shall come forward man by man.

The one who is caught with the things devoted to destruction must be burned, along with all that belongs to him, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD and committed an outrage in Israel.’”

units.label: The exposing of Achan
units.note: my son, give glory to the LORD and confess

verses.text: So Joshua arose early the next morning and had Israel come forward tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was selected.
He had the clans of Judah come forward, and the clan of the Zerahites was selected. He had the clan of the Zerahites come forward, and the family of Zabdi was selected.
And he had the family of Zabdi come forward man by man, and Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was selected.
So Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him. I urge you to tell me what you have done; do not hide it from me.”
“It is true,” Achan replied, “I have sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel. This is what I did:

When I saw among the spoils a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, I {{chamad|coveted}} them and took them. They are hidden in the ground inside my tent, with the silver underneath.”

units.label: Judgment in the Valley of Achor
units.note: why have you brought trouble on us; the LORD turned from His anger

verses.text: So Joshua sent messengers who ran to the tent, and there it all was, hidden in his tent, with the silver underneath.
They took the things from inside the tent, brought them to Joshua and all the Israelites, and spread them out before the LORD.

Then Joshua, together with all Israel, took Achan son of Zerah, the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen and donkeys and sheep, his tent, and everything else he owned, and brought them to the Valley of Achor.
“Why have you brought this trouble upon us?” said Joshua. “Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!” And all Israel stoned him to death. Then they stoned the others and burned their bodies.
And they heaped over Achan a large pile of rocks that remains to this day. So the LORD turned from His burning anger. Therefore that place is called the Valley of Achor to this day.

maal.gloss: To act unfaithfully, to commit a treacherous breach of trust, especially against holy things or against God. Achan's theft is not merely stealing; it is maal, a betrayal of the covenant, a sacrilege against what belonged wholly to the LORD. The word frames the sin as a violation of the relationship between God and His people, which is why it defiles the whole nation.

cherem.gloss: That which is devoted irrevocably to the LORD, set apart for destruction or for His treasury. Jericho and its spoil were placed under the cherem; by taking some for himself, Achan makes himself and, through the covenant bond, the camp of Israel liable to the very ban he violated, so that Israel too becomes set apart for destruction until the devoted thing is removed.

chamad.gloss: To covet, desire, take pleasure in wanting. Achan traces his sin to its root: I saw, I coveted, I took, the very sequence of the fall in Eden and a direct breach of the tenth commandment. The word exposes the inner spring of the sacrilege, showing that the outward theft grew from a heart that desired what God had forbidden.

basic.context: Right after the great victory at Jericho, Israel suffers a humiliating defeat at the small town of Ai, and thirty-six men die. Joshua is devastated and falls before God in prayer. But God tells him the problem is not with God; it is sin in the camp. One man, Achan, had secretly taken some of the plunder from Jericho that had been devoted wholly to the LORD, and hidden it in his tent. Because Israel is one covenant people, that hidden sin brought defeat on everyone. God has the nation brought forward tribe by tribe until Achan is singled out. He confesses that he saw, coveted, and took the forbidden things. Judgment falls in the Valley of Achor, and God's anger is turned away. The question at the heart of it is: why does God take sin among His people so seriously?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and it is one of the hardest chapters in Joshua because Achan's household shares in the judgment. It must be read within its own covenant setting, where the herem was in force and the whole camp had become liable, and not turned into a rule for how communities punish sin today. What endures is its clear teaching: sin is deadly serious, it is never merely private, and God is holy and dwells among His people, so unconfessed sin cannot simply be ignored.
basic.originalLanguages: Achan's act is maal, an unfaithful, treacherous breach against holy things. He took some of the cherem, what was devoted wholly to God. And he names the root: he saw and chamad, coveted, and took, the pattern of Eden and the breach of the tenth commandment.
basic.typology: The Valley of Achor, the place of trouble and judgment, is later promised as a door of hope, Hosea 2:15, pointing to how God turns the place of judgment into a place of renewed hope, ultimately in Christ. Achan bearing judgment for sin against the community throws into relief the one who bears judgment for others to save them.
basic.christ: Achan sinned and brought trouble on the people, and he died for his own sin; Jesus, though sinless, took the trouble of His people upon Himself and died in their place, turning away God's anger not from one man but for all who believe. The Valley of Achor, trouble turned to hope, points to the gospel, where the place of judgment becomes a door of hope in Christ.
basic.god: God is holy and cannot be treated lightly; His anger burns against sacrilege. He is the God of the covenant who binds His people together, so that sin among them is everyone's concern. Yet He is also gracious: He does not abandon Israel but shows them the way back through confession and the removal of sin, and He turns from His anger once the sin is dealt with.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 20 forbids coveting, the root of Achan's sin. Numbers 32 warns that sin will find you out. Hosea 2 turns the Valley of Achor into a door of hope. And 1 Corinthians 5 shows the New Testament church removing sin from among them so the whole body is not defiled.
basic.oneStory: The joy of Jericho gives way to the tragedy of Achan, showing that the greatest threat to God's people is not the enemy outside but sin within. God exposes and removes the sin so He can again be with His people. The Valley of Achor, trouble turned to hope, points forward to Christ, who bears the trouble of His people and opens a door of hope.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 answers chapter 6 point for point in structure as well as content. The previous chapter opens with the LORD's promise, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, and closes on the note that the LORD was with Joshua; this chapter opens instead with the LORD's anger burning against Israel and does not close until that same anger has turned away, verse 26. The two chapters form a matched pair, framing the whole conquest's first movement around a single question, whether the LORD is present with His people or not.

Joshua's prayer, verses 7 to 9, is built on the same shape as Moses' intercession after the golden calf: an anguished why, a fear of what the surrounding nations will conclude, and an appeal to God's own reputation, what will You do for Your great name, mirroring Moses' why should the Egyptians say, Exodus 32:11-12. The narrator expects readers to recognize the pattern and feel the gap between it and God's answer, since Moses is heard pleading for mercy while Joshua is told to get up because the problem is not on God's side at all.

The search that follows, tribe, then clan, then family, then man, uses the very same narrowing device and the same verb, selected, later used for Saul, 1 Samuel 10:20-21, a piece of shared vocabulary that turns a four step search into an unbearable delay before the guilty party is finally named.
context.historical:
Ai lay some fifteen miles from Jericho in the hill country near Bethel, a small town by comparison with the fortress just conquered, which is exactly why the spies' report, few defenders, no need to send everyone, reads as overconfidence bred by the shock of the previous victory rather than careful reconnaissance. Nothing in the text credits their scouting with any fault; the defeat comes entirely from hidden sin in the camp, not poor intelligence, though Israel's own presumption after Jericho set the stage for a humbling surprise.

The phrase rendered acted unfaithfully belonged to a recognized legal category elsewhere in Israel's law, not a vague expression. The same English phrase describes sinning against the LORD's holy things in Leviticus 5:15, which requires a guilt offering and full restitution, and sinning unfaithfully against another person in Numbers 5:6-7, which likewise requires confession and repayment. Achan's sin fits the first category exactly, an offense against property that belonged to God alone, except that no guilt offering could answer it, since the entire city and its plunder had already been placed under an irrevocable ban rather than the ordinary sanctuary economy of offerings and restitution.

Stoning and burning were recognized covenant penalties for grave public offenses, reserved for sins that threatened the whole community's standing before God, and the heap of stones raised over the site turned the valley itself into a lasting, visible warning for every later traveler on the road up from Gilgal.
context.canonical:
A generation later, when the eastern tribes are suspected of covenant breach, the rest of Israel cites this very chapter as a warning precedent: was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful regarding what was set apart for destruction, bringing wrath on the whole congregation, yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin, Joshua 22:20. That later verse settles what this chapter leaves for the reader to absorb, that the household did share the judgment, and that the memory of it was meant to frighten every future generation away from touching what God has set apart.

The test recurs at the very start of the monarchy. Samuel commands Saul to devote the Amalekites and all that is theirs to complete destruction, and Saul instead spares the best of the plunder to sacrifice to the LORD, an excuse eerily close to Achan's own instinct to keep what looked valuable, 1 Samuel 15:3,9,21. Samuel's verdict, to obey is better than sacrifice, and rebellion is like the sin of divination, 1 Samuel 15:22-23, costs Saul his kingdom, exactly as Achan's theft cost him his life, showing that grasping devoted things remained a test Israel's leaders kept failing centuries after Jericho fell.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author has God speak of the whole nation in the singular, Israel has sinned, even though only one household is guilty, forcing first hearers to feel what covenant unity actually costs: they cannot treat Achan's tent as someone else's problem while camped under the same defeat. The command to get up, rather than remain prostrate in grief, is equally deliberate; the narrator wants readers to see that mourning alone changes nothing, and that the road back to God's presence runs through obedient action, consecration, search, and removal, not through prolonged lament by itself.

Above all the author means to teach that God's presence among His people is not an unconditional possession secured once at the Jordan crossing. I will no longer be with you unless you remove the devoted things, verse 12, is meant to unsettle every later reader who assumes past faithfulness guarantees future favor. The chapter's placement, right after the greatest victory yet, drives the point home: proximity to God's mighty acts is no substitute for present holiness, a lesson the author wants carried into every future battle Israel will fight.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The specific mechanism Joshua uses, presenting the nation tribe by tribe until a lot falls on the guilty man, belonged to a unique means available under the old covenant for cases where the LORD Himself needed to expose a hidden offender; it is not a procedure the church is ever told to imitate, and the New Testament instead prescribes patient personal confrontation, Matthew 18:15-17, and reasoned church discipline, 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, wherever sin threatens a congregation. What does transfer is the underlying conviction both testaments share: a community bound to God cannot indefinitely shelter known, unrepented sin without consequence to the whole body, and love for that community sometimes requires exposing what a member would rather keep hidden, precisely so the door back to fellowship can be reopened.

debates.question: Why were Achan's sons and daughters caught up in the judgment?

views.label: Covenant solidarity and likely complicity
views.case: In Israel's covenant world the household was a single unit, and the stolen goods were buried in the family tent, which strongly suggests the family knew and concealed the sin; the judgment falls on a household implicated in hiding what was devoted to God, not on innocents ignorant of the crime.

views.label: A severe covenant sign of sin's corporate reach
views.case: Whatever the family's precise knowledge, the passage dramatizes in the starkest terms that sin is never contained to the individual; its consequences spread outward through the community, a sobering picture the text presents as covenant judgment in a unique moment, not as a model, and one that Deuteronomy 24:16 elsewhere limits by forbidding executing children for a father's sin.

views.label: Read in tension, awaiting the gospel resolution
views.case: Scripture holds together both the corporate reality of sin and the principle of individual responsibility, and this hard episode is not the final word; it presses toward the cross, where One bears the sin of many so that the guilty need not perish, resolving the tension the chapter exposes.

debates.bearing: However one weighs the family's complicity, the passage's abiding point is the terrible seriousness and corporate reach of sin against a holy God, and it drives the reader to long for the substitute who bears sin so others may live.

debates.question: Did Achan's execution itself atone for Israel's sin, or did it simply remove the cause of the LORD's anger?

views.label: Removal, not atonement
views.case: The text never calls Achan's death a sacrifice or offering; it simply obeys the stated condition, remove the devoted thing from among you, verses 12-13, and once the stolen goods and the man who hid them are physically gone from the camp, the LORD turns from His anger, verse 26, exactly as a contaminating object removed from a space restores it, not because Achan's blood paid a debt to anyone.

views.label: A judicial purging that functioned like other covenant purgings
views.case: Deuteronomy repeatedly links capital punishment for grave sins to the command, purge the evil from among you, Deuteronomy 17:7, 19:19, and 21:21, treating the execution itself as the means by which guilt is legally cleared from the land, so Achan's death functions judicially the way a sacrifice functions cultically, clearing guilt rather than merely tidying up stolen property.

debates.bearing: Either way, Achan bears the penalty for his own sin and no more; Scripture never suggests his death benefited anyone besides Israel's immediate deliverance from judgment, which is precisely why the contrast with Christ is so sharp: one man dies for his own guilt, and one Man dies for the guilt of others.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond maal, cherem, and chamad, three more features of the Hebrew repay notice. The verse that indicts Israel piles up four distinct charges for a single act: they have sinned, they have transgressed My covenant, they have stolen, and they have lied, putting the stolen things with their own possessions, verse 11. Hebrew narrative rarely stacks synonyms this thickly; the effect is to show that Achan's one act of grasping fruit and metal was simultaneously a sin against God, a covenant breach, an ordinary theft, and a deception, four charges in a single sentence for a single tent.

The verb behind Achan's own confession, I saw, I coveted, I took, laqach, deliberately repeats the very verb that closes the fall in Eden, she took the fruit and ate it, and gave some to her husband, Genesis 3:6. The narrator wants a reader who knows Genesis to hear the echo: the oldest sin and this new one share not only a shape but a verb, seeing what is desirable and taking it with the hand.

The method by which Achan is finally exposed is never named outright, but Israel's later practice makes it clear enough. The tribe, clan, family, and man are each said to be selected, the same word used of Saul's selection by tribe and clan in 1 Samuel 10:20-21, and the ordinary means behind that word elsewhere in Israel is the goral, the lot, cast before the LORD and trusted to fall exactly where He directs, the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD, Proverbs 16:33. A process that looks like chance to onlookers is, in the narrator's understanding, God's own hand landing precisely on the guilty man.

Finally, the valley itself is renamed by wordplay rather than simple description. Achan, whose name likely echoes the same root as Achor, trouble, gives his name to the very ground where he dies, so the place is called the Valley of Achor to this day, verse 26, and the man becomes, permanently, the trouble he caused. Sin, transgression, theft, deceit; seeing, coveting, taking; a lot cast before the LORD; a name that becomes a place: each piece of the vocabulary presses the same lesson, that this was no small or hidden matter, however quietly it began in one man's tent.

typology.type: The Valley of Achor, the place of trouble and judgment, Joshua 7:26
typology.fulfillment: Hosea takes this exact valley, named for Achan's trouble, and promises that God will one day make it a door of hope, speaking tenderly to His people there as in the days of her youth, Hosea 2:14-15. The valley of judgment becomes, centuries later in prophecy, the very place of restored covenant love, an explicit prophetic reversal rather than a vague echo. Paul states the same principle in different words, where sin increased, grace increased all the more, Romans 5:20; both texts insist that the darkest ground in Israel's story is not too dark for God to remake into hope.

typology.type: Achan bearing judgment so God's anger turns from Israel, Joshua 7:25-26
typology.fulfillment: Achan dies for a sin that was entirely his own, and his death removes the very thing that had brought the whole camp under a curse it did not choose. Christ's death works in the opposite direction: He was pierced for our transgressions, and the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all, though He committed none of it, Isaiah 53:5-6. Paul states the exchange plainly, God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Achan's death answers for his own guilt alone; Christ's death answers for guilt that was never His to begin with.

typology.type: The exposure of hidden sin before the holy God, Joshua 7:16-19
typology.fulfillment: Nothing about Achan's tent is hidden from the God who directs the lot to land on him, tribe by tribe, exactly as Jesus warns that nothing concealed will remain so, for everything hidden will be made known, Luke 12:2-3. John gives the same truth its gentler side, if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness, 1 John 1:9. The two halves of Achan's story, exposure and then judgment, are not the only way that pairing can end; walking in the light with an honest confession lets the very same holy God who exposes also cleanse rather than condemn.

typology.type: Stoning outside the camp for grave sin, Joshua 7:24-25
typology.fulfillment: The law required grave sin to be judged outside the camp, the blasphemer stoned there, Leviticus 24:14, the Sabbath breaker likewise, Numbers 15:35-36, and Achan's own judgment in the Valley of Achor follows the same pattern, sin removed to a place set apart so the camp itself is not defiled. Hebrews takes that pattern and turns it inside out: Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood, and calls believers to go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore, Hebrews 13:12-13. Achan is cast outside the camp because he had defiled it; Jesus goes outside the camp though sinless, so everyone still inside might at last be made clean.

study.christ:
Two silences stand behind this chapter and its gospel counterpart, and they run in opposite directions. Achan says nothing through a full day of tribes, clans, and families being paraded before him, concealing a guilt only the LORD's own lot finally drags into the open; his silence is the silence of hidden guilt, broken only when there is nowhere left to hide. Isaiah describes a very different silence centuries later, oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth, led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7, the silence of a man with no guilt to conceal, accepting an unjust charge without a word in His own defense. Achan is silent because exposure would cost him everything; Christ is silent though He has nothing to hide, because bearing the charge is exactly why He came.

The law that shaped Achan's punishment reaches all the way to Calvary. Grave sin was judged outside the camp, the blasphemer stoned there, Leviticus 24:14, the man who broke the Sabbath likewise, Numbers 15:35-36, and Achan's own judgment in the Valley of Achor keeps to the same pattern, removing sin to a place set apart so the camp itself is not defiled. Hebrews takes that pattern and turns it inside out: Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood, and calls believers to go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore, Hebrews 13:12-13. Achan is cast outside the camp because he had defiled it; Jesus goes outside the camp though sinless, so that everyone still inside might at last be made clean by the very blood that judgment once demanded from the guilty.

Paul draws the exchange out in full: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Achan's death paid only for what Achan himself had done; it purchased nothing for anyone else, and the anger it turned away returned soon enough at the next act of unbelief, Joshua 9. Christ's death, by contrast, answers for sin that was never His, and the anger it turns away is turned away for good.
study.god:
God does not need Joshua's search to learn who sinned; He tells Joshua plainly, before a single tribe is called forward, that Israel has stolen and lied and hidden the things among their own possessions, verse 11. The elaborate process that follows, tribe, clan, family, man, is not detective work for God's benefit but pedagogy for Israel's, making a hidden sin undeniable to an entire watching nation before judgment falls, so that no one could later claim God struck without cause or without warning.

The gravest line in the whole chapter is not the sentence on Achan but God's own warning to the community: I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction, verse 12. Every earlier victory, the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, depended entirely on that presence; losing it, not the army of Ai, is the real catastrophe behind thirty six deaths at the gate. God is teaching that His presence, not Israel's numbers or its weapons, was always the true source of every victory, and that presence cannot simply be assumed to continue regardless of what is tolerated in the camp.

Yet even here patience is threaded through severity. God does not strike the moment the sin occurs; a battle is fought and lost first, a full day of search follows, and Achan is given room, however briefly, to come forward on his own before the lot forces the issue. He does not, and confesses only once cornered, which the text records without softening, yet God's willingness to let a process unfold rather than striking at once shows a God who is in no hurry to condemn, only resolute that sin be dealt with honestly in the end.

And once it is dealt with, His anger genuinely lifts. The chapter does not end with lingering suspicion or a diminished relationship; it ends simply, so the LORD turned from His burning anger, verse 26, a complete and stated reversal. The God who could not be with a camp harboring hidden sin is, in the very next chapter of the story, fully present again for the taking of Ai, proof that His anger, however real, is never the last word for a people who deal honestly with what He has exposed.

crossReferences.note: You shall not covet anything that belongs to your neighbor, the tenth commandment, names the very root Achan later confesses, I coveted them and took them. His theft did not begin when his hand touched the cloak and the silver; it began earlier, in a desire the law had already named and forbidden long before Jericho fell.

Moses warns the tribes settling east of the Jordan, be sure your sin will find you out, long before Achan ever hides anything in his tent. His buried silver and gold prove the warning true within a single generation, dug up from the ground exactly where he thought no one would think to look.

God promises to turn the Valley of Achor, trouble, into a door of hope, and to make His people answer Him there as in the days of their youth. The very ground where Achan died for grasping what was not his becomes, generations later, the site of God's own tender wooing of a repentant people.

Paul asks whether the Corinthians know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough, and tells them to clean out the old leaven so the church can keep the feast with sincerity and truth. Achan is the Old Testament's own case study in exactly this danger, one hidden sin left unaddressed threatening to leaven an entire camp.

Paul says God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. Achan is the reverse picture entirely, a guilty man who dies for his own sin and buys nothing for anyone else, throwing into relief exactly what it cost for Christ to die for sins that were never His.

Years later, when the eastern tribes are suspected of covenant breach, the rest of Israel recalls this chapter by name, was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful, bringing wrath on the whole congregation, yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin. The later verse confirms in plain words what chapter 7 leaves implicit, that the household did share the judgment.

Samuel tells Saul that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that rebellion is like the sin of divination, after Saul spares the best of what should have been devoted to destruction from Amalek. The same test that destroyed Achan costs Saul his throne a generation later, showing that grasping what God has set apart remained a temptation Israel's leaders kept failing.

Ananias keeps back part of the proceeds of a sale while pretending to give it all, and falls dead the moment his deception is exposed before the church, so that great fear comes over all who heard of it. The parallel to Achan is exact in shape though not in era, hidden deception about devoted property, sudden death, and a whole community sobered by what it witnesses.

The woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and she took the fruit and ate it, the same sequence of seeing, wanting, and taking that Achan later confesses almost word for word. His sin in the tent at Ai is the fall in Eden played out again in miniature, on a smaller stage but with the same root.

The Pharisees tell the healed blind man, give glory to God, we know this man is a sinner, using the very words Joshua uses to press Achan toward honest confession. The phrase serves an opposite purpose in each case, an appeal to real repentance in Joshua, a demand for false denial in John, showing the same words can serve either honesty or a lie depending on who is speaking them.

study.oneStory:
Sin entered the world the first time through a man who saw, desired, and took something set apart by God's own word, and death passed on to all men because all sinned, Romans 5:12. Achan's story is that pattern replayed exactly, seeing, coveting, taking, and it costs him his life just as the first sin cost Adam his; between Eden and the Valley of Achor, Scripture keeps insisting that sin is never a private transaction between an individual and temptation, it is always a breach that reaches whoever stands in covenant with the sinner.

Israel has barely begun to receive the promised inheritance, one city taken, when this chapter proves that possessing the land will not, by itself, undo the deeper problem the fall created. A holy God dwelling among an unholy people is a standing danger as much as a promised blessing, and Sinai's law, the tabernacle's furniture, and now this valley all exist to manage that same tension: how the LORD can live among sinners without either abandoning them or destroying them.

The rest of the conquest depends on the answer this chapter gives: expose what is hidden, remove what defiles, and let God's anger turn away once it is dealt with honestly. That pattern repeats through Israel's history, through Saul and Amalek, through kings good and bad, until it finally resolves not in another stoning but in a cross set up outside a different city gate, where the One who bore no devoted thing in His own hand was Himself treated as the devoted thing, cast outside the camp, so that everyone still inside might be made clean, Hebrews 13:12-13.

Revelation ends where this chapter cannot: a new creation where nothing unclean ever enters again, Revelation 21:27, and no curse remains at all, Revelation 22:3. The Valley of Achor, once a place of stones and burning, becomes, in Hosea's promise and in Christ's finished work, proof that no wreckage sin leaves behind is beyond God's power to turn into a door of hope.

quiz.q: Why was Israel defeated at Ai?

options.text: Because Achan had secretly taken things devoted to the LORD, and his hidden sin brought guilt on the whole nation.
options.note: Verses 1 and 11 to 12 name Achan's sin as the cause of the defeat.

options.text: Because the army of Ai was far larger and stronger than Israel expected.
options.note: Ai was actually small; the true cause was sin in the camp, not the enemy's strength.

options.text: Because Joshua failed to pray before the battle.
options.note: The problem was not Joshua's prayer but Achan's hidden sin; God said, Israel has sinned.

options.text: Because God had abandoned His covenant with Israel for good.
options.note: God had not abandoned the covenant; He showed Israel the way back once the sin was removed.

quiz.q: How did Achan describe the way his sin unfolded?

options.text: He saw the plunder, coveted it, and took it, hiding it in his tent.
options.note: Verse 21 traces the sin from seeing to coveting to taking, echoing Eden.

options.text: He took the goods by accident, not realizing they were forbidden.
options.note: It was no accident; he confessed he saw, coveted, and deliberately took and hid them.

options.text: He was ordered by another Israelite to take them.
options.note: No one ordered him; he confessed the coveting was his own.

options.text: He never actually took anything and was falsely accused.
options.note: He confessed the theft, and the goods were found hidden in his tent.

quiz.q: What did God require before He would again be with Israel?

options.text: That they consecrate themselves and remove the devoted thing from among them.
options.note: Verses 12 to 13 make removing the sin the condition of God's renewed presence.

options.text: That they offer a larger army for the next attack on Ai.
options.note: The issue was not army size but removing the sin; a bigger army could not fix a holiness problem.

options.text: That they pay a fine to the town of Ai.
options.note: No payment to Ai was involved; God required the devoted thing be removed from the camp.

options.text: That Joshua step down as leader.
options.note: God told Joshua to stand up and act; the remedy was dealing with sin, not replacing the leader.

quiz.q: What does the tragedy of Achan teach about sin?

options.text: Sin against a holy God is deadly serious and never merely private; it affects the whole community.
options.note: One man's hidden sin brought defeat and death on all Israel, showing sin's corporate reach.

options.text: Sin only matters if it is public and obvious.
options.note: The opposite: Achan's sin was hidden, yet it defiled the whole camp; hidden sin is still deadly.

options.text: Personal sin has no effect on anyone else.
options.note: The chapter shows sin is corporate in its effects; it is never merely private.

options.text: God does not really care about small acts of disobedience.
options.note: God's anger burned over this sin; He takes even hidden disobedience with utter seriousness.

quiz.q: How does the Valley of Achor point forward in Scripture?

options.text: Hosea makes this place of trouble a door of hope, pointing to how God brings grace out of judgment in Christ.
options.note: Hosea 2:15 turns Achor into hope, foreshadowing the gospel reversal at the cross.

options.text: It shows that God's judgment can never be reversed or redeemed.
options.note: The opposite: God later turns this very valley of judgment into a door of hope.

options.text: It teaches that God's people should copy Achan's punishment today.
options.note: The specific covenant judgment is not a model; the church deals with sin through discipline and restoration.

options.text: It has no bearing on the rest of the Bible's story.
options.note: Hosea and the gospel pick up the valley's theme; it points to grace out of judgment in Christ.

questions: Achan's sin was hidden, yet it brought real harm to everyone around him. Where might hidden sin in your life be affecting others more than you realize?
Achan traced his fall to seeing, coveting, and taking. Where do you need to guard your heart against coveting what God has said is not yours?
God would not overlook the sin, but He did show Israel the way back through confession and removal. Is there something you need to bring honestly into the light before God rather than hiding it?
The place of trouble became a door of hope. How does it encourage you that God can bring grace and renewal even out of your worst failures when you turn to Him?
Achan died for his own sin, but Christ bore the trouble of His people to turn God's anger away. How does resting in Christ's substitution free you to confess your sin honestly rather than fearfully?

translationNotes.note: Acted unfaithfully renders maal, a treacherous breach of trust against holy things; the things devoted to destruction render forms of the Hebrew cherem, as the BSB footnote notes, recurring in verses 11, 12, 13, and 15.
Achan means troubler, as the BSB footnote notes; he is also called Achar in 1 Chronicles 2:7, tying his name to the trouble he caused.
The cloak from Shinar is a luxury import from Babylonia, as the BSB footnote notes; the silver and gold are given in shekel weights the footnotes convert to modern measures.
The Valley of Achor means trouble, as the BSB footnote notes, tying the place to Achan the troubler and to Joshua's word about trouble.
